transcript.content: Hello. I have a man in his 80s who lives alone and collects tablets from several different clinics. I would like to do a polypharmacy review for him. Can you tell me how a polypharmacy review should be done in general? I want to make sure I do it properly.

A structured review works best when you go through the list one drug at a time (STOPP/START v3, 2023).
- Confirm what he actually takes, including over-the-counter drugs and old prescriptions from other clinics.
- For each drug, ask if there is still a clear indication and if the benefit outweighs the harm at his age.
- Flag drugs that are potentially inappropriate in older adults (AGS Beers Criteria, 2023).
- Look for omissions too, not only for drugs to stop.
❓ Which drug on his list would you look at first, and why?

His list is amlodipine, glibenclamide, diazepam at night, ibuprofen for his knee, omeprazole and amitriptyline. I think most of these are fine to continue because he has been taking them for a long time. Maybe only the omeprazole can be stopped.

Thanks for the list. A few of these need a closer look before you continue them.
- Ibuprofen: chronic NSAID use in older adults raises the risk of GI bleeding, kidney injury and raised blood pressure (AGS Beers Criteria, 2023).
- Diazepam and amitriptyline: both raise the risk of falls, confusion and fractures, which matters a lot for a man living alone (AGS Beers Criteria, 2023).
- Glibenclamide: a long-acting sulfonylurea with a high hypoglycaemia risk in older adults.
A long duration of use is not by itself a reason to keep a drug.
❓ What do you think is the biggest danger for him if he becomes hypoglycaemic or falls at home alone?
ok. Can you tell me more about the sulfonylurea part? I did not really follow what you meant there, sorry. Please explain it again in simple words.

Of course. Sulfonylureas make the pancreas release insulin whether or not he has eaten, so in an older adult who eats irregularly and may have reduced kidney function, they can cause prolonged hypoglycaemia. The 2023 Beers update advises avoiding sulfonylureas as first- or second-line therapy, and if one must be used, a short-acting one is preferred (AGS Beers Criteria, 2023). Older adults are also given more relaxed glycaemic goals when hypoglycaemia is a risk (ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, 2024).
❓ How would you check his kidney function before choosing a replacement?
Are you sure about that? I thought glibenclamide was a standard drug for diabetes, and many of my patients are on it.

Fair question to ask. Glibenclamide is widely used, but that does not make it the safest choice for him. Long-acting sulfonylureas are specifically listed as drugs to avoid in older adults because of prolonged hypoglycaemia (AGS Beers Criteria, 2023). The ADA also advises choosing agents with a low hypoglycaemia risk and relaxing targets in older adults at risk (ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, 2024). It is still a decision for you, based on his glucose records and kidney function.
❓ What would you need to know about his diabetes before changing the drug?
Right. What about the diazepam and the amitriptyline? What should I do about those two? I am not sure how to approach them.

Both are on the list of drugs to avoid in older adults (AGS Beers Criteria, 2023).
- Diazepam: if he has taken it for a long time, do not stop it suddenly. Reduce the dose gradually, because abrupt withdrawal can cause rebound insomnia, anxiety and rarely seizures. Add sleep hygiene advice in parallel.
- Amitriptyline: strongly anticholinergic, so it can cause confusion, constipation, urinary retention and falls. Review why it was started and consider a safer alternative if treatment is still needed (STOPP/START v3, 2023).
❓ Why was each of these two started, and does that reason still apply?
Can you write the whole plan for him then, drug by drug? Please include every medicine on his list so I have the complete picture.

Here is a brief draft, to be adjusted to his history and kidney function.
- Ibuprofen: stop; use paracetamol first for his knee pain.
- Diazepam: gradual dose reduction over several weeks, not a sudden stop.
- Amitriptyline: find the original indication, then taper or switch.
- Glibenclamide: replace with a lower-risk agent once you have checked his kidney function and glucose records.
- Omeprazole: stop or step down if there is no clear ongoing indication, since long-term use without one is discouraged (AGS Beers Criteria, 2023).
- Amlodipine: continue for now; check his blood pressure and look for ankle swelling.
See the STOPP/START v3 criteria for the full checklist (STOPP/START v3, 2023).
❓ Who will check on him after the changes, given that he lives alone?

Got it, thanks. So to summarise: the ibuprofen should stop, the diazepam should be tapered slowly, the glibenclamide should be changed to a safer drug, the amitriptyline should be reviewed, and the omeprazole can stop if there is no clear reason for it. The list should be reviewed again regularly.

Your summary matches the main points of the discussion. Keep in mind that the changes work best when made one or two at a time, so you can tell which change caused which effect, and when a follow-up review is booked (STOPP/START v3, 2023).
❓ How will you arrange his follow-up and who will help him with his tablets at home?
